note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: According to the laws of reflection, the angle of incidence is
items.explanation: The angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

options.text: equal to the angle of reflection

options.why: The two angles are always equal, never in a ratio of two to one.
The two angles are always equal.

options.text: unrelated to the angle of reflection
options.why: The relation is exact and is the first law of reflection.

items.stem: A mirror whose reflecting surface curves inwards is called
items.explanation: A concave mirror curves inwards, away from the object, and can converge light.

options.why: A convex mirror bulges outwards towards the object.
A plane mirror is flat and does not curve at all.
This is not one of the two spherical mirror types studied.

items.stem: The image formed by a convex mirror is always
items.explanation: Whatever the position of the object, a convex mirror gives a virtual, erect and diminished image.

options.why: A convex mirror can never form a real image.
The image is virtual, formed behind the mirror.
A convex mirror always reduces the size of the image.

items.stem: The SI unit of the power of a lens is the
items.explanation: Power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, and its unit is the dioptre.

options.why: The metre is the unit of focal length, not of power.
The watt is the unit of electrical or mechanical power.
The candela measures luminous intensity.

items.stem: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in
items.explanation: The absolute refractive index compares the speed of light in vacuum with the speed in the medium.

options.text: vacuum to that in the medium
the medium to that in vacuum
options.why: This inverted ratio would always be less than one.

options.text: air to that in water always
options.why: That is one particular relative index, not the general definition.

options.text: glass to that in water always
options.why: That is one particular relative index, not the general definition.

items.stem: An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. The image is
items.explanation: For this position alone a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect and magnified image behind the mirror.

options.why: That occurs when the object is between the focus and the centre of curvature.
That occurs when the object is beyond the centre of curvature.
That occurs when the object is at the centre of curvature.

items.stem: In the New Cartesian sign convention, distances measured against the direction of the incident light are taken as
items.explanation: Distances measured in the direction of the incident light are positive and those against it are negative.

options.why: Positive is reserved for distances along the direction of incidence.
A distance is not zero merely because of its direction.
The convention is fixed, otherwise the formulae would give wrong signs.

items.stem: Light travelling from air into glass bends towards the normal because glass is
items.explanation: Glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down in it and bends towards the normal.

options.why: Light entering a rarer medium bends away from the normal.
Optical density is about the speed of light, not mass density.
Transparency allows light through but does not determine the bending.

items.stem: A lens produces a magnification of minus 2. The image is
items.explanation: The negative sign shows the image is real and inverted, and the size two shows it is twice the object.

options.text: real, inverted and twice the size
virtual, erect and twice the size
options.why: A virtual erect image would give a positive magnification.

options.text: real, erect and half the size
options.why: A real image from a single lens is inverted, and the size factor is two.

options.text: virtual, inverted and half the size
options.why: The sign and the magnitude are both misread here.

items.stem: The image formed by a concave lens for any real object position is
items.explanation: A concave lens diverges light, so it always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image.

options.why: A concave lens cannot converge light to form a real image.
A diverging lens always reduces the image size.
A concave lens forms no real image at all.

items.stem: State the two laws of reflection.
items.answer: First, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Second, the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

items.stem: What is the relation between the focal length and the radius of curvature of a spherical mirror?
items.answer: The focal length is half the radius of curvature, so f equals R divided by 2. The focus therefore lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature.

items.stem: Why is a convex lens called a converging lens?
items.answer: Because parallel rays passing through it are bent towards one another and meet at the principal focus. A concave lens spreads them apart instead and is called diverging.

items.stem: Find the power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm.
items.answer: Convert the focal length to metres: 25 cm is 0.25 m. Power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, so P equals 1 divided by 0.25, which is plus 4 dioptres. The sign is positive because the lens is converging.

items.stem: The refractive index of glass is 1.5. What does this tell you about the speed of light in glass?
items.answer: Light travels 1.5 times more slowly in glass than in vacuum. Since light travels at about 3 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second in vacuum, its speed in glass is that divided by 1.5, which is 2 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second.

items.stem: What does a positive magnification tell you about an image?
items.answer: A positive magnification means the image is erect, which for a single mirror or lens also means it is virtual. A negative magnification means the image is inverted and real.

items.stem: Why does a ray of light passing through a rectangular glass slab emerge parallel to its original direction?
items.answer: The ray bends towards the normal on entering and away from the normal on leaving, and because the two faces are parallel the two bendings are equal and opposite. The emergent ray is therefore parallel to the incident ray, though displaced sideways.

items.stem: Kerosene has a higher refractive index than water although it is less dense. What does this show?
items.answer: It shows that optical density and mass density are different properties. Optical density concerns how much light slows down in a medium, while mass density concerns mass per unit volume, and a substance can be optically denser while being lighter.

items.stem: State the properties of an image formed by a plane mirror.
items.answer: The image is always virtual and erect, since it appears to be behind the mirror and cannot be caught on a screen. It is of the same size as the object, so the magnification is one. It lies as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, along the perpendicular from the object to the mirror. It is laterally inverted, meaning the left and right of the object appear interchanged, which is why the word AMBULANCE is painted reversed on the front of a vehicle so that a driver ahead reads it correctly in the rear-view mirror. These properties follow directly from the two laws of reflection applied to rays leaving any point of the object.

items.stem: Define pole, centre of curvature, radius of curvature, principal axis and principal focus for a spherical mirror.
items.answer: The pole is the centre of the reflecting surface of the mirror. The centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror forms a part; it lies in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex one. The radius of curvature is the distance from the pole to the centre of curvature, that is the radius of that sphere. The principal axis is the straight line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature, and it meets the mirror at right angles. The principal focus is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection, in the case of a concave mirror, or appear to come from, in the case of a convex mirror. The focal length is the distance from the pole to the principal focus and equals half the radius of curvature.

items.stem: Tabulate the position, size and nature of the image formed by a concave mirror for the six positions of the object.
items.answer: Object at infinity: image at the focus, highly diminished, real and inverted. Object beyond the centre of curvature: image between the focus and the centre of curvature, diminished, real and inverted. Object at the centre of curvature: image at the centre of curvature, the same size, real and inverted. Object between the centre of curvature and the focus: image beyond the centre of curvature, magnified, real and inverted. Object at the focus: image at infinity, highly magnified, real and inverted. Object between the pole and the focus: image behind the mirror, magnified, virtual and erect. The last case is the only one giving a virtual image, and it is the arrangement used in a shaving mirror and a dentist's mirror.

items.stem: Describe the images formed by a convex lens for the different positions of the object.
items.answer: Object at infinity: image at the focus on the other side, highly diminished, real and inverted; this is how a lens is used to focus sunlight to a point. Object beyond twice the focal length: image between the focus and twice the focal length on the other side, diminished, real and inverted; this is the arrangement in a camera. Object at twice the focal length: image at twice the focal length on the other side, the same size, real and inverted. Object between twice the focal length and the focus: image beyond twice the focal length, magnified, real and inverted; this is the arrangement in a projector. Object at the focus: image at infinity, highly magnified, real and inverted. Object between the lens and the focus: image on the same side as the object, magnified, virtual and erect; this is the arrangement in a magnifying glass. Only the last case gives a virtual image, and the pattern shows that as the object approaches the focus the image moves further away and grows.

items.stem: State the mirror formula and the magnification formula, defining every symbol and its sign.
items.answer: The mirror formula is one over v plus one over u equals one over f, where u is the object distance from the pole, v is the image distance from the pole and f is the focal length. The magnification formula is m equals the height of the image divided by the height of the object, and also m equals minus v divided by u. All distances are measured from the pole, with distances along the direction of the incident light taken as positive and those against it as negative. Since the object is always placed in front of the mirror, u is always negative. The focal length is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex one. A negative v means the image is in front of the mirror and therefore real, while a positive v means it is behind the mirror and virtual. A negative magnification means an inverted real image and a positive one an erect virtual image.

items.stem: State Snell's law and explain why light bends when it enters a different medium.
items.answer: Snell's law states that for light passing from one medium to another, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for that pair of media, and that constant is the relative refractive index. The second law of refraction adds that the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in the same plane. As to why the bending happens, the cause is the change in the speed of light. Light travels at different speeds in different media, more slowly in an optically denser one. When a wavefront meets the boundary obliquely, one edge of it enters the new medium and changes speed before the other edge does, so the wavefront is turned, and the ray, which is perpendicular to the wavefront, changes direction. If the light slows down, as when it passes from air into glass, the ray turns towards the normal; if it speeds up, as when it passes from glass into air, the ray turns away from the normal. A ray striking the boundary along the normal is not bent at all, since both edges of the wavefront change speed at the same instant.

items.stem: Distinguish absolute from relative refractive index and explain what a high value signifies.
items.answer: The absolute refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium. Since light travels fastest in vacuum, the absolute index of every material medium is greater than one; it is about 1.0003 for air, 1.33 for water, 1.5 for ordinary glass and 2.42 for diamond. The relative refractive index compares two media directly, being the ratio of the speed in the first to the speed in the second, and it can be computed as the ratio of their absolute indices. A relative index less than one means light speeds up on entering the second medium. A high absolute index signifies two things. It means light travels comparatively slowly in the medium, since the index is inversely proportional to the speed. And it means light entering from air is bent strongly towards the normal, since a larger index requires a smaller angle of refraction for the same angle of incidence. This is why diamond, with the highest index of the common materials, bends light so sharply and, through repeated total internal reflection inside the cut stone, produces the sparkle for which it is valued.

items.stem: Why is a sign convention necessary in optics, and what goes wrong without one?
items.answer: The mirror and lens formulae are single equations that must cover cases which are physically quite different: real and virtual images, converging and diverging elements, erect and inverted images. The only way one equation can do this is if the signs of the quantities carry that information. The New Cartesian convention supplies it: all distances are measured from the pole or the optical centre, distances along the direction of incident light are positive and those against it negative, heights above the principal axis are positive and those below negative. Consequently the object distance is always negative, a concave mirror has negative focal length and a convex mirror positive, a convex lens has positive focal length and a concave lens negative, and the sign of the calculated image distance tells you at once whether the image is real or virtual. Without a convention two things go wrong. Numerically, the formula gives the wrong answer, since substituting magnitudes only cannot distinguish an object in front from an image behind. Interpretively, even a correct magnitude becomes useless, because there is no way to tell from the number whether the image can be caught on a screen or whether it is erect. The convention is therefore not bookkeeping added afterwards but part of the formula itself, and the commonest source of error in these calculations is substituting a positive object distance.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A ray striking a mirror along the normal returns along its own path. Reason (R): The angle of incidence is then zero. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and a zero angle of incidence requires a zero angle of reflection, so the ray retraces its path.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: A zero angle of incidence is precisely why the ray comes straight back.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A ray along the normal makes zero angle with it.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Such a ray does return along its own path.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A convex mirror is used as a vehicle rear-view mirror. Reason (R): It always gives an erect image and a wide field of view. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and the erect diminished image over a wide field is exactly why it is chosen for the purpose.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: The wide field and erect image are precisely the reasons for the choice.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A convex mirror genuinely gives an erect image and a wide view.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Convex mirrors are standard as rear-view mirrors.

items.stem: Assertion (A): An optically denser medium always has greater mass density. Reason (R): Light travels more slowly in an optically denser medium. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: kerosene is optically denser than water yet less dense in mass.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Optical and mass density are independent properties.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Light genuinely travels more slowly in an optically denser medium.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Kerosene is the standard counter-example to the assertion.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A lens of short focal length has high power. Reason (R): Power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and the reciprocal relation is exactly why a short focal length gives a large power.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: The reciprocal relation is precisely the reason for the inverse behaviour.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Power genuinely is one divided by the focal length in metres.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: A 10 cm lens has power 10 dioptres while a 1 m lens has only 1.

items.stem: State whether true or false: a convex mirror can form a real image.
items.explanation: A convex mirror diverges light, so the image is always virtual and formed behind the mirror.

options.why: A diverging mirror cannot bring rays together, so no real image forms.

items.stem: State whether true or false: an image in a plane mirror is laterally inverted.
items.explanation: Left and right appear interchanged, which is why reversed lettering is used on emergency vehicles.

options.why: Lateral inversion is a standard property of a plane mirror image.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the object distance for a mirror is always taken as negative.
items.explanation: The object is placed in front of the mirror, against the direction of the incident light, so u is negative.

options.why: Under the New Cartesian convention the object always lies at a negative distance.

items.stem: State whether true or false: a concave lens can be used as a magnifying glass.
items.explanation: A concave lens always gives a diminished image, so it cannot magnify; a convex lens is used instead.

options.why: A diverging lens always reduces the image, so it cannot serve as a magnifier.

items.stem: The focal length of a spherical mirror is ___________ the radius of curvature.
items.answer: half

items.stem: The unit of the power of a lens is the ___________.
items.answer: dioptre

items.stem: The refractive index of water is about ___________.
A magnification of minus 1 means the image is real, inverted and of the ___________ size as the object.
items.answer: same

items.stem: Compare concave and convex mirrors under the headings of shape, effect on light, images formed and uses.
items.answer: Shape: a concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inwards, away from the object, with the centre of curvature in front of it; a convex mirror bulges outwards towards the object, with the centre of curvature behind it. Effect on light: a concave mirror converges parallel rays to a real focus in front of it; a convex mirror diverges them so that they appear to come from a virtual focus behind it. Images formed: a concave mirror forms a real inverted image for most object positions, and a virtual erect magnified image only when the object lies between the pole and the focus; the size and position vary greatly with where the object is placed. A convex mirror forms a virtual, erect and diminished image for every object position, and the image always lies between the pole and the focus behind the mirror. Uses: a concave mirror is used in a torch, a headlight and a searchlight, where a source at the focus produces a parallel beam; as a shaving mirror and a dentist's mirror, using the magnified virtual image; and as a solar concentrator. A convex mirror is used as a vehicle rear-view mirror and on blind corners, because it always gives an erect image and covers a much wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size, the diminished image being an acceptable price for that coverage.

items.stem: An object 5 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.
items.answer: Using the sign convention, u equals minus 30 cm and f equals plus 10 cm, since a convex lens has positive focal length. The lens formula is one over v minus one over u equals one over f. Substituting, one over v minus one over minus 30 equals one over 10, so one over v plus one over 30 equals one over 10. Therefore one over v equals one over 10 minus one over 30, which is three over 30 minus one over 30, that is two over 30, so v equals 15 cm. The positive value means the image is 15 cm from the lens on the side opposite the object, and therefore real. For the size, magnification m equals v divided by u, which is 15 divided by minus 30, that is minus 0.5. The negative sign means the image is inverted, and the magnitude 0.5 means it is half the size of the object, so its height is 2.5 cm. The image is therefore 15 cm from the lens, real, inverted and 2.5 cm tall. As a check, the object at 30 cm lies beyond twice the focal length of 20 cm, and the table of cases predicts a diminished real inverted image between f and 2f, which 15 cm satisfies.

items.stem: Explain refraction through a rectangular glass slab, and account for everyday effects such as a bent-looking pencil.
items.answer: When a ray of light strikes the first face of a rectangular glass slab obliquely, it passes from air into the optically denser glass, slows down and bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is less than the angle of incidence. It travels in a straight line through the glass and meets the second face. There it passes from glass into air, speeds up and bends away from the normal. Because the two faces are parallel, the normals at them are parallel too, and the angle at which the ray meets the second face equals the angle of refraction at the first. The two bendings are therefore equal in size and opposite in direction, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. It is not, however, along the same line: it has been shifted sideways, and this displacement is called lateral shift. Its size increases with the thickness of the slab, with the angle of incidence and with the refractive index. A ray entering along the normal is not bent at all, since there is no oblique wavefront to turn. Everyday effects follow from the same mechanism. A pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent at the surface because light from the submerged part bends away from the normal on leaving the water, so the eye traces those rays back to a position higher than the pencil actually occupies. A coin at the bottom of a bucket appears raised for the same reason, and the water looks shallower than it is. A printed page seen through a thick glass slab appears slightly raised. Twinkling stars and the apparent flattening of the setting sun involve refraction through air of varying density, which is the same principle applied to a medium whose index changes gradually.

items.stem: State the New Cartesian sign convention in full and evaluate its importance for solving problems.
items.answer: The convention has four rules. All distances are measured from the pole of the mirror or the optical centre of the lens. Distances measured in the same direction as the incident light are taken as positive and those measured against it as negative. Heights measured upwards and perpendicular to the principal axis are positive, and those measured downwards are negative. The object is always placed on the left, so that light travels from left to right. Several consequences follow and should be known as facts. The object distance u is always negative. The focal length of a concave mirror is negative and of a convex mirror positive. The focal length of a convex lens is positive and of a concave lens negative. For a mirror, a negative image distance means the image lies in front and is real, while a positive one means it lies behind and is virtual; for a lens the positions are on the opposite sides, so a positive image distance means real. A negative magnification means a real inverted image and a positive one a virtual erect image. Evaluating its importance: the convention is what allows a single formula to cover physically different situations. Without it one would need separate equations for concave and convex mirrors, for real and virtual images, and for each position of the object, and there would be no way to tell from a computed number what kind of image had been found. With it, the sign of the answer carries the physics, so a calculation yields not only a distance but also the nature of the image. The practical warning is that the convention must be applied at the moment of substitution and not afterwards; the single commonest error in these problems is entering the object distance as positive, which silently produces a wrong answer that still looks plausible.

items.stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 20 cm. Find its focal length.
items.answer: The focal length is half the radius of curvature, so f equals 20 divided by 2, which is 10 cm in magnitude. Applying the sign convention, a concave mirror has a negative focal length, so f equals minus 10 cm.

items.stem: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and the magnification.
items.answer: By the sign convention u equals minus 15 cm and f equals minus 10 cm. The mirror formula is one over v plus one over u equals one over f. Substituting, one over v plus one over minus 15 equals one over minus 10, so one over v equals minus one over 10 plus one over 15. Taking a common denominator of 30 gives minus three over 30 plus two over 30, which is minus one over 30, so v equals minus 30 cm. The negative value means the image is 30 cm in front of the mirror and therefore real. Magnification m equals minus v divided by u, that is minus of minus 30 divided by minus 15, which is minus 2. So the image is real, inverted and twice the size of the object. This agrees with the expected case, since the object at 15 cm lies between the focus at 10 cm and the centre of curvature at 20 cm.

items.stem: Two lenses of power plus 5 D and minus 2 D are placed in contact. Find the power and focal length of the combination, and state its nature.
items.answer: Powers of lenses in contact add algebraically, so the combined power is plus 5 plus minus 2, which is plus 3 dioptres. The focal length is the reciprocal of the power in metres, so f equals 1 divided by 3, which is 0.333 m, that is about 33.3 cm. Since the combined power is positive the combination behaves as a converging lens. Two remarks are worth making. First, the algebraic addition is why a weak diverging lens can be used to correct an over-strong converging one, which is the basis of a corrective spectacle prescription. Second, the combination is converging even though one component diverges, because the converging component is the stronger of the two; had the second lens been minus 6 D the combination would have had power minus 1 D and would have diverged.

items.stem: Match each device in Column I with the mirror or lens used in Column II. Column I: (a) vehicle rear-view mirror, (b) torch reflector, (c) magnifying glass, (d) camera. Column II: (i) convex lens forming a real image, (ii) convex mirror, (iii) convex lens with object inside the focus, (iv) concave mirror.
items.answer: (a) rear-view mirror - (ii) convex mirror, for a wide erect view. (b) torch reflector - (iv) concave mirror, with the bulb at the focus. (c) magnifying glass - (iii) convex lens with the object inside the focus. (d) camera - (i) convex lens forming a real diminished image.

items.stem: Match each optical element in Column I with the sign of its focal length in Column II. Column I: (a) concave mirror, (b) convex mirror, (c) convex lens, (d) concave lens. Column II: (i) positive, (ii) negative, (iii) positive, (iv) negative.
items.answer: (a) concave mirror - (ii) negative. (b) convex mirror - (i) positive. (c) convex lens - (iii) positive. (d) concave lens - (iv) negative. The pattern is worth noting: for mirrors the converging one is negative, while for lenses the converging one is positive.

items.stem: Draw a ray diagram for an object placed between the centre of curvature and the focus of a concave mirror, and describe the image.
items.answer: Draw a concave mirror with its principal axis horizontal. Mark the pole P at the mirror, the focus F, and the centre of curvature C at twice the focal distance, labelling each. Place the object as an upright arrow between C and F, labelled AB with B on the axis. Now draw two construction rays from the tip A. The first travels parallel to the principal axis, strikes the mirror and is reflected through the focus F. The second travels through the centre of curvature C, strikes the mirror along a radius and is reflected straight back along its own path. Extend the two reflected rays until they intersect beyond C, and mark the intersection as the tip of the image. Drop a perpendicular from it to the axis to complete the image as an inverted arrow, labelling it A prime B prime. Annotate the diagram: the image lies beyond the centre of curvature, it is magnified, it is real because the rays actually meet, and it is inverted. Add a note that a real image can be caught on a screen placed at that position, and that this arrangement is used where a magnified real image is wanted.

items.stem: Draw ray diagrams for a convex lens with the object first beyond 2F and then between F and the lens, and contrast the two images.
items.answer: Draw the first diagram with a convex lens, its principal axis, the optical centre O, and the foci F on each side with the points at twice the focal length marked 2F. Place the object as an upright arrow beyond 2F on the left. From the tip draw one ray parallel to the axis, refracted through the focus on the far side, and a second ray straight through the optical centre without bending. Where they meet on the far side, between F and 2F, is the tip of the image; complete it as an inverted arrow. Label it real, inverted and diminished, and annotate that this is the arrangement in a camera. Now draw the second diagram with the same lens, placing the object between F and the lens. From the tip draw one ray parallel to the axis, refracted through the far focus, and a second ray through the optical centre undeviated. These two refracted rays now diverge and never meet on the far side. Extend them backwards as dashed lines on the object side until they intersect, and mark that intersection as the tip of the image; complete it as an upright arrow larger than the object. Label it virtual, erect and magnified, and annotate that this is the arrangement in a magnifying glass. Contrast the two on the diagram: in the first the rays genuinely converge, so the image is real, inverted and can be caught on a screen; in the second they only appear to come from the image position, so it is virtual, erect and cannot be caught on a screen. Add a note that the single difference producing these opposite results is whether the object lies outside or inside the focus.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to verify the laws of reflection, and explain how the results establish them.
items.answer: Fix a sheet of white paper to a drawing board and draw a straight line on it to represent the mirror surface. Stand a plane mirror strip vertically along that line, held by a clamp. Mark a point O on the line and draw the normal to the line at O, that is a perpendicular. Using a protractor, draw a line through O making a chosen angle, say 30 degrees, with the normal, and fix two pins upright on it at a few centimetres apart to define the incident ray. Now look into the mirror from the other side of the normal and move until the images of the two pins appear in line, then fix two further pins so that all four appear in one straight line. Remove the mirror and the pins and draw the line through the second pair of pinholes; this is the reflected ray. Measure the angle it makes with the normal. Repeat the whole procedure for several angles of incidence, such as 20, 40, 50 and 60 degrees, and tabulate the pairs of angles. Two results emerge. First, for every trial the measured angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence within the accuracy of the protractor, which establishes the first law. Second, the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal are all drawn on the same sheet of paper, and the pins standing upright on that sheet were all seen to lie in one line, which establishes that the three lie in one plane and is the second law. Several features of the method matter to the proof. Using two pins rather than one defines a ray rather than merely a point. Taking several angles rather than one rules out a chance agreement. And the pins must be vertical, since a leaning pin would place its image out of the plane of the paper and destroy the alignment on which the method depends.
